reason: Tempting because Deuteronomy 18:15-19 is the prophet-like-Moses oracle that 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes and that this corpus uses repeatedly, and because 26:1 is about words Christ will speak that 'shall be the law which ye shall do'. But the shared string is a relative clause of pure connective tissue, and Deuteronomy 18:19's subject is the requiring of obedience from those who will not hearken, not the giving of a new law. If Deuteronomy 18 is in view here it has left no verbal trace; the adjudicated link for that oracle sits at 1 Nephi 22:20.

Malachi 4 is genuinely in view in this chapter, but at 26:4 and 26:6 (v. 1) and 26:9 (v. 2), not here. Malachi 4:3's treading down of the wicked as ashes shares only a connective run with 26:3, whose sources are Genesis 4:10 and the Abel-to-Zacharias tradition of Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:50-51.

Nephi's 'whirlwinds shall carry them away' and Isaiah 41:16's 'the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them' share the idiom and split the two winds differently. The image of chaff or stubble taken by a whirlwind is distributed across Isaiah 17:13, 40:24, 41:16 and Job 21:18, and no one of them can be identified as the source. Recorded because the verse's neighbours do borrow from Isaiah and a reader may expect this clause to as well.

The sense is opposed. Psalm 71:20 is a promise of rescue — 'shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth' — and 26:5 has the depths of the earth swallowing the killers of the prophets. The nearer image is Korah at Numbers 16:32, where the earth opens her mouth and swallows them up, and that is recorded as composite on the Hosea 10:8 row.

'Anger kindled against' is one of the KJV's commonest formulas of judgment — eleven verses have 'the anger of the LORD was kindled' alone. Deuteronomy 31:17 has 'my anger shall be kindled against them in that day', which matches Nephi's tense; but the link at this verse is to Isaiah 5:25, whose participial 'the anger of the LORD kindled' is a KJV singleton and which Hardy cross-references here alongside the stubble.
Four words of the same formula, from the episode of Miriam's leprosy. Superseded by the Isaiah 5:25 row at this verse.

A real rarity pointed at the wrong verse, and worth the entry. 2 Kings 10:30 is the Lord's reward to Jehu — 'thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel' — a dynastic promise with no bearing on Nephi's four generations of righteousness before destruction. The formula Nephi is using is the Decalogue's 'unto the third and fourth generation' (Exodus 20:5, Numbers 14:18, Deuteronomy 5:9), which he inverts from a reach of punishment into a span of reprieve, and which is catalogued as a link at this verse. Note that Exodus 20 returns at 26:32.
Connective. Qoheleth's subject is the prosperity of sinners; Nephi's is the certainty of a foreseen destruction. The link at this verse is to Isaiah 52:3.

'It must needs be' is one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest connectives and appears throughout 2 Nephi 25-30. Matthew 18:7's subject is offences. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A six-word run and a real one: John 20:31 is the Fourth Gospel's statement of purpose, 'that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God', and 26:12 twice says that Jews and Gentiles must be convinced 'that Jesus is the Christ'. But the clause is the New Testament's standard confession and appears at Acts 9:22, 17:3, 18:5, 18:28 and 1 John 5:1; the distinctive word in Nephi's sentence is 'very', which points at Acts 9:22 and John 7:26, and the link is filed there. Recorded here because a reader who knows Frederick's work on Johannine language in the Book of Mormon might expect John 20:31 to be claimed at this verse, and this catalogue declines to claim it.
'By the power of God' is a KJV commonplace. The link at this verse is to Revelation 14:6's fourfold list of nations, kindreds, tongues and peoples.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:3-5 at 26:14, which introduces the prophecy ('But behold I prophesy unto you concerning the last days') without quoting anything. The wording begins in the next verse and runs through three: Isaiah 29:3's camp, siege and forts at 26:15, Isaiah 29:4's voice out of the ground at 26:16, and Isaiah 29:5's chaff and instant at 26:18. CONVENTIONS §6a: the links sit where the wording is and this entry sends the reader from his verse to all three. This is not drift in our extraction — his reference is a chapter-level pointer placed at the head of a passage, which is what a study edition's apparatus is for.
Narrative boilerplate; Saul's relief of Jabesh-gilead. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1.
Connective. Paul is delivering the institution of the supper; Nephi is asserting that the Lord God worketh not in darkness — a clause whose real relative is John 3:19, catalogued at 26:10.

Five words of formula. Isaiah 50:4 is the servant's tongue of the learned, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 7:4 — which makes the match worth naming and rejecting rather than passing over, since a reader may suspect the transcription is being reused. It is not: 26:30's source is 1 Corinthians 13.

Connective, though Job 34:28's 'cry of the poor' is thematically adjacent to 26:20's grinding upon the face of the poor. The shared words carry none of that, and the invitation formula in 26:33 is Matthew 11:28's.

sharedText: the day that cometh shall burn them up
reason: Hardy keys Malachi 4:1 to both 26:4 and 26:6, and the wording is at 26:4 — “all they that are proud, and that do wickedly, the day that cometh shall burn them up”, which is Malachi's sentence almost entire. 26:6 has the visitation and the destructions but none of Malachi's words. The link is at 26:4 and cites him there (CONVENTIONS §6a: the link goes where the wording is, and the register sends the reader from his verse to ours).
